about.title: Arithmetic Sequences as Linear Functions
about.length_note: About 30 minutes, which fits a half-hour class. The class has two rules (recursive and explicit) and then one link to lines. The beats are short, with a check after each new idea. Stop after any beat and pick up there next time if you need to.

sources.title: High School: Functions, Interpreting Functions (standards HSF-IF.A.3 and HSF-IF.B.5)
Chapter 13 key concepts: Arithmetic Sequences (Algebra and Trigonometry 2e)
Formulas for Arithmetic Sequences (College Algebra with Corequisite Support)
Arithmetic & Geometric Sequences: Recursive & Explicit Formulas (Algebra 1)

say.text: Today we look at number patterns that grow by the same amount every step, and we turn them into a rule.

show.text: Patterns that add the same amount

say.text: A sequence is just a list of numbers in order. Each number in the list is called a term.

show.text: Sequence = a list of numbers in order. Each number is a term.

say.text: Say Sam starts a game day with 20 coins and earns 15 more each day. His coins at the end of each day are 20, 35, 50, 65.

show.text: Day 1: 20 coins. Then 35, 50, 65 ...

say.text: The same number, 15, gets added every time. That is what makes this an arithmetic sequence.

show.text: Arithmetic sequence: each term is the previous term plus a constant. That constant is the common difference, d.

say.text: To find d, take any term and subtract the one just before it. Here 35 minus 20 is 15, and 50 minus 35 is 15 too.
Your turn. Look at 50, 44, 38, 32. Subtract each term from the next one. What is d?

ask.q: What is the common difference of 50, 44, 38, 32?
ask.why: Next term minus previous term: 44 − 50 = −6, and 38 − 44 = −6 too. The sequence goes down, so d is negative.

say.text: Careful: the differences must all match. Take 2, 4, 8, 16. The jumps are 2, then 4, then 8.

show.text:
4 − 2 = 2
8 − 4 = 4
16 − 8 = 8
The jumps differ, so this is NOT arithmetic.

ask.q: Which list is an arithmetic sequence?
ask.why: 3, 7, 11, 15 adds 4 every time. The others have jumps that change: 3, 6, 12, 24 jumps by 3, 6, 12, and 1, 2, 4, 7 jumps by 1, 2, 3.

say.text: Now for the first rule. A recursive rule says where you start, and how to get each term from the one before.

show.text: Recursive rule: a₁ = start, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d

say.text: For Sam's coins, the start is 20, and each new day is the day before plus 15. We write a₁ = 20 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 15.

ask.q: A sequence has a₁ = 7 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 3. What is a₃?
ask.why: a₂ = 7 + 3 = 10, then a₃ = 10 + 3 = 13. You have to go through a₂ to reach a₃.

say.text: There is one problem with the recursive rule. To get the 50th term, you need all 49 terms before it.

show.text: Recursive means you need the previous term first, so term 50 takes 49 steps.

say.text: The explicit rule fixes that. You plug in the term number n and get that term straight away.

show.text: Explicit rule: aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1)

say.text: Why n − 1? To get from term 1 to term n, you make n − 1 jumps. Each jump adds d.

show.text:
Term 1 to term 4 = 3 jumps
3 = 4 − 1
So a₄ = 20 + 15·3 = 65 ✓

say.text: Now the 10th day. Nine jumps of 15 from 20 gives a₁₀ = 20 + 15(9) = 155 coins. We did not need the first nine days.

ask.q: The sequence is 5, 8, 11, 14, ... Use aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1). What is a₂₀?
ask.why: a₁ = 5 and d = 3. So a₂₀ = 5 + 3(19) = 62. Using 20 in place of 19 gives 65. That is the usual slip.

say.text: To write the explicit rule from a list, do two things. Find d, then put d and the first term into the formula.

show.text:
1. d = a₂ − a₁
2. aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1)
3. Simplify if you like

say.text: Try 20, 35, 50. Here d = 15, so aₙ = 20 + 15(n − 1). Distribute and combine: 20 + 15n − 15, which gives 15n + 5.

show.text: Before simplifying: aₙ = 20 + 15(n − 1)  |  After simplifying: aₙ = 15n + 5

say.text: A quick check: put n = 1 into 15n + 5. You get 20, which is the first term. So the rule works.
Here is the big link. A sequence is a function. The input is the term number n, and the output is the term.

show.text: Sequence = a function. Input: n (1, 2, 3, ...). Output: the term.

say.text: The inputs are only whole numbers, like 1, 2, 3. There is no day 2.5, so the domain is a set of whole numbers, not every number.

show.text: The domain of a sequence is a subset of the integers.

say.text: Look at Sam's coins as points: day 1, 20 coins; day 2, 35 coins; and so on. The dots line up in a straight line.

show.text: Sam's coins by day

say.text: That is because an arithmetic sequence has a constant rate of change. That makes it a linear function.

show.text: Arithmetic sequence = linear function on whole-number inputs

say.text: The common difference is the slope. Look at aₙ = 15n + 5. It matches y = mx + b, with m = 15 and b = 5.

show.text:
y = mx + b  |  aₙ = 15n + 5
m = slope = d = 15

ask.q: A sequence has the rule aₙ = 4n + 3. What is its common difference?
ask.why: In a rule that looks like mx + b, the number on n is the slope. For a sequence, the slope is the common difference, so d = 4.

say.text: What about the +5? It is what you would have on day 0, before the first day. Textbooks sometimes start at term 0 for this reason.

show.text:
Start at term 1: aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1)
Start at term 0: aₙ = a₀ + dn
Here a₀ = 5

say.text: Sequences can go down too. Say your phone battery is 100%, then 96%, 92%. Now d = −4, so the line slopes down.
Notice that the rule is 104 − 4n, not 100 − 4n. Check n = 1: 104 − 4 = 100 ✓. If we used 100 − 4n we would get 96 for term 1, which is wrong.

ask.why: Here d = −3 and a₁ = 30. So aₙ = 30 − 3(n − 1) = 33 − 3n. Check n = 1: 33 − 3 = 30 ✓. The rule 30 − 3n gives 27 for n = 1, so it is wrong.

say.text: Let's pull it together. Find d. Write the recursive rule or the explicit rule. And see that d is the slope of a line.

show.text:
d = next − previous
Recursive: a₁ = start, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d
Explicit: aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1)
d = slope; inputs are whole numbers

say.text: Nice work today. Coming up, we look at functions made of pieces, and at how to shift and flip graphs.

show.text: Next class: Piecewise and Absolute Value Functions

other_side.claim: The explicit rule for an arithmetic sequence is written aₙ = a₁ + d(n − 1), counting from term 1.
other_side.other_view: Textbooks do not all count from term 1. In application problems, OpenStax says the formula is sometimes changed to start at term 0, as aₙ = a₀ + dn. This is useful when the starting amount is the value before any steps. Both forms give the same sequence. Use whichever one your class or test uses.
